memorial_note: Bismarck is a war grave. About 2,100 crew died when she sank on 27 May 1941. Observe, photograph and leave the wreck undisturbed.

entries.title: Bismarck: the last battle
paragraphs: Bismarck was one of the largest battleships ever built by Germany, commissioned in August 1940. In May 1941 she sailed into the North Atlantic with the heavy cruiser Prinz Eugen on Operation Rheinubung, a commerce raid intended to disrupt Allied shipping. The Royal Navy intercepted her, opening a three-day pursuit that became one of the most famous naval actions of the Second World War.

On 24 May 1941, at the Battle of the Denmark Strait, Bismarck and Prinz Eugen engaged HMS Hood and HMS Prince of Wales. Hood was destroyed in minutes, with all but three of her 1,419 crew lost; Bismarck took damage that forced her to abandon the raid and head for occupied France for repairs. Swordfish torpedo bombers from HMS Victorious and, on 26 May, from HMS Ark Royal found and struck her; a torpedo hit near the stern jammed her rudders, leaving her unable to steer clear of the pursuing British fleet. On the morning of 27 May, HMS King George V and HMS Rodney closed in and bombarded her for almost two hours. With the ship ablaze, listing, and unable to fight back, her crew opened the sea cocks and detonated scuttling charges; she sank, stern-first, at roughly 10:40. Of her crew of 2,221, only around 114 were rescued -- most by HMS Dorsetshire and HMS Maori, who broke off the rescue early on report of a U-boat sighting.
Robert Ballard’s team found the wreck on 8 June 1989. Later expeditions documented the hull, detached structures and debris with submersibles and remotely operated vehicles.

Published surveys place Bismarck at about 4,790 m. This dive uses the 2001 expedition’s published vicinity, where the terrain grid reads about 4,219 m. The roughly 570 m gap between that grid and the survey remains unresolved; the hull stays on the seabed shown here.

entries.title: Upright on the seamount
paragraphs: Bismarck rests upright on the south face of an extinct undersea volcano. Much of the hull survives, embedded in sediment, while the stern has broken away. The 2001 expedition photographed the surviving bow, empty gun barbettes and damaged upper decks.

The falling hull struck the slope and slid before settling. An impact crater, a long slide scar and detached structures trace that final journey. The 2001 survey describes a slide of roughly 1.5 km on a 14.5° slope.
Surviving teak decking and protective paint remain visible in survey images, alongside shell damage and corrosion.

entries.title: The main gun turrets
paragraphs: Bismarck’s four main-battery turrets, Anton, Bruno, Caesar and Dora, each carried two 38 cm guns. The turrets fell out of their barbettes as the ship capsized and sank, landing separately on the slope.
Ballard’s 1989 team found one turret. The 2001 expedition identified another, tentatively called Caesar, near the hull. Their empty barbette rings remain a striking feature of the wreck.

facts.value: Anton, Bruno, Caesar, Dora — 4 x twin 38 cm

entries.title: Shellfire, torpedoes, or scuttling?
paragraphs: By the morning of 27 May 1941, Bismarck could no longer steer or fight back effectively: a torpedo hit near the stern the evening before had jammed her rudders, and HMS King George V and HMS Rodney closed to point-blank range and battered her for nearly two hours. With the ship ablaze and listing heavily, her crew opened the sea cocks and set off scuttling charges below decks, and she went down stern-first around 10:40.

Survey teams have reached different conclusions about the final sinking. David Mearns’s 2001 expedition attributed it to combined battle damage and flooding, with scuttling hastening the end; James Cameron’s 2002 team emphasized scuttling. Both documented a heavily damaged wreck.

facts.label: Final bombardment
facts.value: 27 May, HMS King George V and HMS Rodney

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: debated: battle damage, scuttling, or both

entries.title: An extinct undersea volcano
paragraphs: The seamount rises northeast of the hull, from about 4,219 m to about 4,024 m over roughly 3 km in this terrain grid. Detached-turret markers sit upslope along the route.

The 2001 expedition’s images show an impact crater and a much steeper slide scar at the actual wreck site. The broad grid relief here gives the setting, while those survey images document the wreck’s last movement.

facts.value: 4,790-4,791 m (deeper than this tile reads here)

entries.title: A war grave
paragraphs: Bismarck went down with roughly 2,100 of the 2,221 men aboard her. HMS Dorsetshire and HMS Maori pulled about 110 survivors from the freezing water before breaking off, on the report of a possible U-boat; a few more were later picked up by a German weather ship and U-boat. It remains one of the largest single losses of life in the Battle of the Atlantic.
Treat the wreck as a memorial: observe its structure and learn its history while leaving it undisturbed.

facts.label: Status
facts.value: treated as a war grave by every expedition
